questions.q: Define situational irony and give one example from "The Enemy" where the outcome is the opposite of what the characters or readers expect.
questions.a: Situational irony occurs when the actual outcome of a situation is starkly different from what was expected or intended. In "The Enemy," Dr. Sadao is a Japanese patriot trained in America who initially wants to hand over the American POW, but his medical training (American) compels him to save the enemy's life — the very skills he learned from the "enemy" nation make him betray his own country's wartime expectations. A wrong answer that only defines irony without a text-specific example reveals the student cannot connect the abstract term to concrete textual evidence, a critical gap for board exam answers.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the fog/mist functions as a symbol in the opening pages of the story. What abstract idea does it represent beyond its literal weather description?
questions.a: The fog symbolizes moral ambiguity and the blurring of boundaries between "enemy" and "human." It hides the injured man's identity initially, just as war propaganda hides the shared humanity of opposing sides. When the fog lifts, Sadao must confront the reality — a white man, an American, his enemy — yet his professional duty cuts through the national "fog." A wrong answer that treats the fog only as atmospheric description misses its symbolic function, showing the student reads literally rather than analytically, which loses marks in both board and competitive exam questions on symbolism.

questions.q: Identify an instance of dramatic irony in the General's conversation with Sadao (pages 39-40). What does the reader know that Sadao does not, and how does this create tension?
questions.a: Dramatic irony occurs when the reader knows the General has forgotten his promise to send assassins (revealed on page 45), but Sadao spends three nights in terror expecting them. The reader knows the General's self-absorption ("I thought of nothing but myself") while Sadao believes the plan is in motion. This creates tension because Sadao's actions — keeping the partition open, losing sleep — are based on a false premise. A wrong answer that confuses dramatic irony with situational irony or misses the General's forgetfulness shows the student cannot track knowledge gaps between characters and reader, a skill tested in CUET and board inference questions.

questions.q: Compare the symbolism of the sea in the opening (bringing the wounded man) and the ending (the escape route to the island). How does the sea's symbolic meaning shift across the narrative?
questions.a: Initially, the sea is a threatening force that "flings" the enemy onto Sadao's shore — an unwelcome intrusion of war into domestic space. By the end, the same sea becomes a pathway to freedom; the unfortified island reachable by boat represents a neutral space beyond national jurisdiction. The sea transforms from a barrier separating nations to a connector enabling humanitarian escape. A wrong answer that treats the sea only as setting or gives identical meanings for both instances fails to trace symbolic evolution, which is required for higher-order analysis questions in board exams and JEE-style literary reasoning.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "The surgical instruments are the most important symbol in the story because they represent Sadao's divided loyalty." Defend or refute with textual evidence.
questions.a: The statement is partially defensible but incomplete. The instruments do symbolize Sadao's professional identity (American-trained) cutting through national allegiance — he uses them to save the enemy. However, the quilt (Japanese tradition covering the "dirty" enemy), the flashlight (hope/guidance), and the scars on the prisoner's neck (evidence of torture, shared suffering) are equally significant. The instruments alone cannot capture the story's full symbolic architecture. A wrong answer that simply agrees without nuance shows an inability to evaluate competing symbolic weights, a skill needed for CBSE competency-based "evaluate" questions.

questions.q: Write a 4-line paragraph from the perspective of the old gardener, using verbal irony to express his true feelings about Sadao saving the American. The character should say the opposite of what he means.
questions.a: "Oh, what a magnificent deed our master performs — healing the very enemy who bombs our cities, while his own countrymen die untreated. Truly, his American education has taught him the finest patriotism: save the foe, betray the fatherland. The moss garden will flourish with such noble fertilizer." A poor answer that has the gardener speak sincerely or uses situational instead of verbal irony reveals the student cannot distinguish irony types or adopt a character's voice, both tested in creative writing sections of board exams.
